newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges schools to raise learning standards.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges schools to raise learning standards.

text.p: Setting a fast pace early in his second term, President Clinton visited innovative Midwestern schools Wednesday and urged educators throughout the United States to match them in raising learning standards.

"Education has been at the heart of America's progress for over 200 years," Clinton said in a speech at Glenbrook North High School in this suburban Chicago community. He added that U.S. wealth and power would "increasingly be measured in the minds and creativity of our people."

Glenbrook and Stanley Field Middle School, which Clinton had visited earlier, belong to a consortium of Chicago area public schools that proved they were among the best in the world in a 1996 international test of math and science skills.

Clinton, who says improving U.S. education is one of his top second-term priorities, challenged other school districts to set and maintain rigorous standards in math and science and compare their performance with schools in 41 other nations by applying to take the Third International Math and Science Study (TIMSS) test in 1997 or 1998.

"We have the best higher education system in the world, there's no question about it. But we do not have the best system of education in the world from start to finish for all of our children, and we cannot be satisfied until that is exactly what we have," he said.

He said the federal government would help offset the cost of the tests with funds from the Education Department, which will work in conjunction with the National Science Foundation, under the Goals 2000 school improvement programme. Aides said Clinton's new budget, to be submitted to Congress Feb. 6, will call for a 26 percent increase in these funds, raising the annual amount available from $491 million to $620 million.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton's turning of public attention to successful schools was the "quintessential use of the bully pulpit" -- the president's power to persuade -- and said the country was likely to see more of the same during the next four years.

"One change in the president's conduct of the presidency itself in the second term versus the first term is that we won't be oriented all the time on what's happening in Congress, on what's happening in legislation," McCurry said.

Clinton seems bent on keeping the political initiative. On Tuesday, he offered a Medicare spending concession to congressional Republicans to sweeten upcoming negotiations on a balanced budget agreement and said his Democratic Party would unilaterally adopt some campaign finance reforms.

The schedule for Clinton's visit to Illinois also included a meeting with Chicago Mayor Richard Daley and the Chicago School Board, which has taken innovative steps to improve city schools, borrowing in some cases from parochial schools.

While the whirlwind trip was designed to build on the momentum from Clinton's inaugural Monday, it conveniently got the president out of Washington on a day when anti-abortion groups are marking with a series of protests the 24th anniversary of a Supreme Court ruling that legalised abortion.
